opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually quite cyclical, and maybe that's the healthy way for it to be. When you first get into this field, there's a kind of naive excitement — you see a model do something you didn't think was possible, and it feels like magic. For me, some of that came early, when I was working on things like Transformer-XL and XLNet. You'd train a model and suddenly it could handle longer context or understand language in a way that felt qualitatively different. That was a very pure kind of excitement.

But then you go through phases where the excitement fades a bit, because you start to see the limitations very clearly. You realize the model is still making silly mistakes, or that scaling a certain direction gives you diminishing returns. And honestly, those periods are important, because that's when you think hardest about what's actually missing.

Then something new happens — a new paradigm, like when we saw what large-scale pretraining could do, or more recently with reasoning and reinforcement learning, where the model starts to think for longer and solve problems it couldn't before — and the excitement comes back, but it's a different kind. It's less about "wow, this is magic," and more about "okay, I can see the path now, I can see how this compounds."

So I'd say the excitement doesn't really decrease; it changes its texture. Early on it's surprise. Later it's more like conviction. You get excited not because something looks impressive in a demo, but because you understand why it works and you can see that it's going to keep getting better. And I think that second kind is actually more durable — it's what keeps you going through the stretches when progress looks flat from the outside.

r001.rationale: The response says excitement fades as limitations become clearer, but does not identify becoming accustomed to AI as the cause.

r002.rationale: It describes new AI paradigms and improved reasoning capabilities renewing excitement.

r003.rationale: It says excitement does not decrease overall and describes cycles of fading and renewal, but does not attribute that stability to habituation counterbalanced by AI progress.

fable-5.1.text:
I think my excitement has actually gone up and down in waves, and each wave feels different from the last one.

The first wave was around 2014, 2015, when I was starting my PhD at CMU. Deep learning was just taking off, and the feeling then was mostly curiosity. You could take some neural network, apply it to a language problem, and get a result that was clearly better than what people had done for twenty years. That was exciting in a very personal way, like you had found a cheat code. But honestly, if you had asked me then whether this would lead to AGI, I would have said probably not in my lifetime.

Then there was a period where things got a bit flat. Around 2018, 2019, we were doing things like Transformer-XL and XLNet, and we could see that scale mattered, but the field felt like it was in a race to add one more point on a benchmark. The excitement became a bit more professional and less emotional. You know how to make progress, but you also start to see the ceiling.

What changed that for me was watching what happened with GPT-3 and then with ChatGPT. It wasn't just that the models got bigger. It was that the same simple principle, next token prediction plus scale, kept working far past where most people thought it would. For me that was the moment the question flipped from "can this work" to "how far does this go." That's a different kind of excitement. It's less about a clever trick and more about a long road that you can now actually see.

And now I would say my excitement is calmer but much deeper. It's less like a fan watching a game and more like a builder who knows the next ten steps. Some days you feel the pressure of competition, the cost of compute, all the practical things. But underneath that, I think the core belief has become stronger rather than weaker. I used to get excited by individual results. Now I'm excited by the direction, and the direction doesn't change week to week.

So if I had to summarize: it went from curiosity, to a kind of professional rhythm, to a real conviction. And conviction is a quieter emotion than curiosity, but it lasts a lot longer.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a flatter period and a shift toward professional rhythm, but does not say that becoming accustomed to AI caused the decline.

r002.rationale: The candidate says GPT-3 and ChatGPT renewed excitement because AI capabilities kept improving beyond expectations, shifting the question to how far they could go.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes excitement changing in waves and a stronger current conviction, but does not connect habituation and AI progress as opposing effects that keep overall excitement relatively stable.

astra-6.text:
I think my excitement moves in cycles, but the underlying conviction keeps growing. When a new idea starts working, you get very excited because you suddenly see possibilities that weren’t visible before. Then you spend a long time dealing with the details, and you discover that turning that possibility into something useful is much harder than it first appeared.

For me, those two stages bring different kinds of excitement. One is the surprise of a breakthrough. The other is the satisfaction of understanding something more deeply and making steady progress. Over time, I think I’ve become less dependent on the first kind. There are still moments that feel extraordinary, but what sustains me is having an important problem to work on and seeing a path toward solving it.

r001.rationale: The response says Yang has become less dependent on breakthrough excitement, but does not identify becoming accustomed to AI as a cause of declining excitement.

r002.rationale: It describes excitement when a new idea works, but does not identify rapid improvements in AI capabilities as a source of renewed excitement.

r003.rationale: The response describes excitement moving in cycles and conviction growing, but does not attribute relative stability to opposing effects of habituation and AI progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my excitement changes as my understanding changes. Early on, you can be excited by the broad idea that AI might do something extraordinary. Then, when you work on it, you see the limitations and how much effort it takes to make even a small improvement. Your expectations become more grounded.

But occasionally, something works that you didn’t quite believe would work, and that brings a different kind of excitement. It’s more concrete: you can see a new possibility and start asking what it would take to get there. So, for me, it’s less a steady increase or decrease and more a cycle of possibility, hard work, and surprise.

r001.rationale: The response says hands-on experience reveals limitations and grounds expectations, but it does not identify becoming accustomed to AI as the cause of declining excitement.

r002.rationale: It describes occasional surprising successes that renew excitement, but does not identify rapid improvements in AI capabilities as the source.

r003.rationale: The response describes a cycle of possibility, hard work, and surprise, but does not explain that habituation and AI progress offset each other to keep excitement relatively stable overall.
